title: R on Longleaf
text:
Conditions for a successful job
Before submitting, verify that the script uses correct file paths, required packages are available, the working directory is intentional, and the requested time and memory are realistic.

title: Introduction to Longleaf
text:
Estimated time: 5 minutes
Guiding question: When does a research problem belong on Longleaf rather than a laptop?

title: Introduction to Longleaf
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this module, participants should be able to:

describe Longleaf in plain language;
identify research tasks that benefit from shared computing resources; and
explain where Longleaf fits between a personal computer and a cloud service.

title: Introduction to Longleaf
text:
Why researchers outgrow laptops
Frame Longleaf around familiar research constraints: analyses that take too long, datasets that exceed local memory, repeated models that can run independently, or work that must continue after a laptop is disconnected.

title: Introduction to Longleaf
text:
What Longleaf is
Introduce Longleaf as a shared computing cluster: many computers coordinated so researchers can request the processing time, memory, and software needed for a particular job.

title: Introduction to Longleaf
text: A brief history and context

title: Introduction to Longleaf
text:
Key takeaway
Longleaf is not simply a faster personal computer. It is a shared system where work is described as a job, assigned resources, and scheduled to run on an appropriate compute node.

title: Getting Started with Longleaf
text:
This workshop follows the path from first login to a submitted R job. The five modules are designed for a 45–60 minute presentation and remain available afterward as a practical reference.
Audience: Researchers who are new to Longleaf or shared computing clusters
Format: Five short modules with demonstrations and reusable examples

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
text:
Estimated time: 8 minutes
Guiding question: What happens between logging in and a computation actually running?

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this module, participants should be able to:

distinguish a login node from a compute node;
explain what a scheduler and queue do; and
interpret basic requests for CPUs, memory, and time.

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
text:
The path through a cluster


1 · Connect
Begin from a laptop, terminal, or browser.


2 · Prepare
Use a login node to organize files and describe the job.


3 · Schedule
Slurm places the request in a queue and finds suitable resources.


4 · Compute
A compute node runs the job and writes its output.

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
text:
What is a node?
A node is an individual computer within the cluster. Introduce the distinct roles of login nodes and compute nodes before discussing detailed hardware.

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
text:
What is a queue?
Explain that a queue is how a shared cluster orders work while matching each job to the resources it requested.

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
section: What does memory mean on a cluster?
text:
What does memory mean on a cluster?
Connect memory requests to the size and behavior of the analysis. Emphasize that requesting more memory reserves capacity but does not automatically make code faster.

title: Key Features of Computing Clusters
text:
Key takeaway
Users describe the work and resources it needs; the scheduler decides when and where that work runs.
